item.title: Evolutionary Insights into the Serenity Prayer
item.description:
Evolutionary Psychology

Evolutionary Insights into the Serenity Prayer

Evolutionary psychology can provide wisdom on behavior that is changeable.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • Evolutionary psychology can help us understand which human dispositions we can and cannot change.
  • Learning changes the brain, showing that biology and experience are intertwined rather than opposites.
  • Understanding evolved tendencies may help us channel them constructively instead of trying to eliminate them.
  • Accepting biological limits can help us focus our efforts on changes that are realistically achievable.

The Serenity Prayer

During the 1930s, theologian Reinhold Niebuhr began incorporating into his sermons what is now known as the Serenity Prayer. In 1941, Alcoholics Anonymous adopted this familiar version:

God give me the serenity
To accept the things I cannot change
Courage to change the things I can
And wisdom to know the difference

Although the AA version emphasizes divine assistance, the heart of the prayer is the wisdom to distinguish what can be changed from what cannot. Without such wisdom, people may waste enormous time and energy trying to change what is impossible to change. Can psychology help us discern what we can and cannot change?

Wisdom from Psychology

Martin Seligman addressed this question in his book What You Can Change and What You Can't. Although published in 1993, its central message remains sound. Seligman explains how our evolved biology places important constraints on psychological change and why disorders such as anxiety and depression are highly treatable while disorders such as post-traumatic stress disorder are extremely difficult to treat.

People sometimes want to change ordinary personality traits rather than clinical problems. Many hope to become more conscientious or extraverted. Research reviewed by Peter Haehner and colleagues (2024) shows that intentional personality change is possible to some extent. However, biology limits how far those changes can go. Understanding those limits can help us set realistic goals.

Biology Guarantees and Constrains Change

Many discussions of psychological change assume that biologically based traits are fixed because we carry the same genes throughout life while learned traits are changeable because they can be unlearned. This distinction is misleading for several reasons. I have described these reasons in detail in a previous post. I will summarize two of these reasons below.

First, learning itself is a biological process. Whenever we learn, our brains change. If nothing changes in the brain, nothing has been learned.

Second, genes do not simply create fixed, unchanging characteristics. Throughout life, they guide development, becoming activated or deactivated by both internal and environmental conditions. From infancy through old age, humans undergo profound psychological and behavioral changes made possible because genes have built brains capable of learning. Biology therefore makes change possible rather than preventing it.

At the same time, biology imposes limits. Humans will never sprout wings and fly. Less dramatically, extreme introverts are unlikely to become extreme extraverts. If we seek wisdom about what can and cannot be changed, biology deserves careful attention.

Resistance to Biological Constraints

Many people resist the idea of biological constraints because they seem to threaten personal freedom or social equality. Historically, some biological theories were indeed misused to justify racism, sexism, and other forms of inequality.

During the 1970s, critics of sociobiology—the forerunner of modern evolutionary psychology—argued that sociobiology served conservative political agendas by portraying social hierarchies as natural and inevitable. Similar criticisms continue today.

Yet surveys consistently find that evolutionary social scientists tend to lean politically left rather than right. Moreover, many evolutionary psychologists argue that the real source of resistance to discussions about biology is not politics but commitment to the "blank slate" view of the human mind—the belief that people are born without important behavioral predispositions. This perspective offers comforting reassurance that people can become almost anything through learning alone. In effect, it rejects the Serenity Prayer's premise that some aspects of human nature cannot be changed.

A New Book on Evolutionary Constraints

I recently read Hunter Trace's The Why Behind Things, which summarizes key insights from several decades of work by evolutionary psychologists, biologists, and anthropologists. Among its most important themes are:

  • We are often unaware of why we do what we do.
  • Many of our hidden motives evolved during millions of years when humans lived in small ancestral groups.
  • Some of these motives are enduring features of human nature.
  • Traits that once promoted flourishing may be poorly suited to modern environments.
  • Rather than trying to ignore or eliminate evolved tendencies, we should design environments that channel them in healthier directions.

These ideas illustrate how evolutionary psychology might provide some of the wisdom sought by the Serenity Prayer. Instead of struggling to erase enduring aspects of human nature, we should learn to work with them.

Political Tribalism

Political polarization offers a useful example. Americans increasingly identify with opposing political tribes, often displaying hostility, disrespect, and sometimes violence. How should we respond? The blank slate perspective suggests that tribalism is entirely learned. If the blank slate perspective is true, education could teach people not to think tribally.

Evolutionary psychology offers a different approach. Throughout human history, our ancestors lived in tribes that frequently competed with other tribes. We may therefore possess evolved tendencies to identify strongly with groups, where learning determines which particular groups we identify with. This is similar to our evolved capacity for language and learning the specific languages we are exposed to.

If this evolutionary perspective is true, attempting to eliminate tribal identification by teaching people not to think tribally may be unrealistic. A more promising strategy might be to help people recognize these evolved tendencies and channel them into less destructive forms of competition and cooperation.

Working With Human Nature

Hunter Trace hopes readers will use evolutionary insights to replace self-defeating habits with healthier ways of thinking and living. Denying biological influences will not eliminate problems such as unhealthy eating, compulsive gambling, excessive moralizing, avoidance of challenges, or compulsive screen use. Instead, understanding these tendencies in their evolutionary context can help us develop more constructive ways of managing them. This approach reflects one of my own long-standing goals: improving individual lives and society by applying insights from evolutionary science.

Trace proposes five broad principles:

  • Discover evolutionary truths about human nature.
  • Design environments that fit those realities.
  • Tell stories that give meaning without encouraging victimhood or demonizing others.
  • Cultivate humility.
  • Resist paralysis in the face of human imperfections and incomplete knowledge.

No strategy guarantees a perfect future. But accepting the realities of human nature while thoughtfully shaping the environments in which people live might offer our best hope for improving both individual well-being and society.

item.title: So, Your Partner Won't Take a Vacation. Now What?
item.description:
Career

So, Your Partner Won't Take a Vacation. Now What?

The hidden motivations behind avoiding vacation and how to work with them.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • Idleness aversion means people crave a reason to stay busy, not that they don't value rest.
  • Busyness signals status and self-worth, so arguing for rest fights a social reward.
  • Overwork past 55 hours adds minimal output, so give rest purpose, not just permission.
Source: AI-Generated

You've probably already tried the obvious approach. You've told that special person "you deserve this," pointed out how tired they look, maybe even booked something and hoped they'd relax once they arrived. But it didn't work, or it worked for about a day before they went berserk checking email and worrying about work FOMO while at the beach. If you love someone who treats a day off like getting a tooth pulled rather than a reward to be enjoyed, the problem isn't that they don't recognize the value of rest. It's that the argument doesn't touch what's actually driving their behavior. Here's what's happening and what you can do about it.

What's happening inside

What's often going on in the brain is something researchers call "idleness aversion," a fancy way to describe a person who cannot sit still. Hsee et al. (2010) demonstrated how aversion works in practice. They gave participants a choice. Drop off a survey at a distal location and walk away, or drop it off in an adjacent office and simply wait 15 minutes with nothing to do. Most people given even a flimsy excuse to stay busy walked away, and the busy group reported feeling better afterward than those in the group who chose to sit and do nothing. The pattern held even when people were forced into the decision rather than just choosing it (Hsee et al., 2010). The researchers concluded that people don't dread effort so much as they dread idleness without justification, and they'll accept almost any outcome rather than sitting still. Your partner's brain isn't necessarily longing to achieve goals, it's seeking permission to stay in motion.

This reframes a lot of what looks like "can't relax." It usually isn't anxiety, and it usually isn't a character flaw. Unstructured time genuinely registers as painful for a lot of people, not because something is wrong with them, but because they've rarely practiced tolerating it. Busyness, meanwhile, has a lifetime of benefits: praise, promotions, and the distraction of not having to sit ruminating on their own thoughts, which may feel worse than dedicating effort to work. Each is a reward from the brain's perspective. What matters most is that reward histories can be changed, but not through arguments, the typical approach most frustrated partners use to stimulate change.

Why arguing doesn't work

There's a second hidden layer that weakens the "you deserve a break" argument. Bellezza et al. (2017) found that in some cultures a leisure-free schedule functions as a status signal. Telling people how busy you are implies you're competent, in demand, and hard to replace, which increases the person's self-esteem (Bellezza et al., 2017). Your partner isn't just avoiding discomfort when they skip a vacation. They may also be, consciously or not, protecting something that resonates with them and others as evidence of personal value.

This also explains why the workaholic label can be revered. Elon Musk advocates that meaningful impact requires 80 sustained work hours a week, and former Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer has described 130-hour weeks at Google as a matter of strategically timing sleep and bathroom breaks. Both are textbook examples of status-signaled busyness functioning exactly as Bellezza et al. (2017) predicted: hard work is a badge of honor rather than a burden. But the highly productive corporate superstar is a productivity myth that doesn't hold up to empirical scrutiny. Pencavel (2014) found that productivity per hour declines sharply after about 50 hours, and after roughly 55 hours, additional time does not generate productivity gains. Someone working 80 hours is often getting no more done than someone working 55. The 80-hour work week isn't a productivity strategy; it's an ego booster and a great rationalization when your idleness-aversive partner wants to reason away your vacation request and justify their need for permission to stay in motion (Hsee et al., 2010). This is why arguing fails. You're arguing against a genuine discomfort with rest while also fighting the exact social reward and personal recognition your partner craves. "You deserve a break" feels like punishment when productivity may be the only thing they find truly rewarding.

What actually helps

Instead of the "chill out" narrative, give rest a justification instead of asking for its absence. According to Hsee et al. (2010), people resist unstructured idleness but will agree to take on activities framed as purposeful. A trip with a specific itinerary, a place to be, or something to see, will succeed where "let's just relax" won't. Even if you can't convince your partner that rest will boost their work performance, you may win acceptance by showing them the benefit to you. If nothing else, they might concede just to stop hearing your nagging.

Use small steps. A long, open-ended vacation can feel more threatening to someone who relies on busyness than a tightly scheduled three-day trip. Build an itinerary around their preferences, their favorite food or drink, or a chance for leisure fitness. Watch your own language. For someone whose identity is wrapped up in being indispensable, try "maybe you don't want a vacation, but your co-workers might want one from you." Curiosity also works better than demands. Ask your partner what they think would actually happen if they took time off. The fear underneath, that they'll fall behind or be seen as replaceable, is usually more tractable than the behavior itself.

Model the benefits of rest. Whillans (2020) found that people who protect free time are happier, healthier, and often more productive than those working more hours. Getting off the grid, rather than checking in, is one of the most underused ways to increase well-being, according to Whillans. If you take the trip and come back visibly better for it, that will do more than any argument ever could. None of this makes the wait easy. But it reframes the question in a more useful way. You're not fighting your partner's laziness or their disregard for their own well-being. You're up against a reward system that's been reinforced for years, and reward systems change through better rewards, not through better arguments.

item.title: Transpersonal Psychology: The Field That Died and Won
item.description:
Psychology

Transpersonal Psychology: The Field That Died and Won

Personal Perspective: Transpersonal psychology didn't survive as a field but as a diaspora.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • Transpersonal psychology is widely treated as a fringe field within academic psychology.
  • Its core preoccupations of altered states, mysticism, and spirituality did not disappear but migrated.
  • A field can lose its institutional home and still win the argument it was making.

Transpersonal psychology is usually spoken of in the past tense. Ask a psychology graduate student what it is, and you will likely get a shrug, maybe a vague reference to Maslow or Grof if they are historically astute, or maybe you’ll get a joke about the 1960s and 1970s.

The flagship journals in transpersonal psychology arguably have a fraction of the readership they once did, and few doctoral programs still bear the name. The professional associations that once anchored the field have thinned considerably. By some institutional measures, transpersonal psychology looks like a field that is dying.

Source: Kevin Turcios / Unsplash

Nonetheless, almost everything transpersonal psychology was preoccupied with is now mainstream. Psychedelic-assisted therapy is studied at some of the most prestigious universities in the world now. Contemplative neuroscience and mind-body research have their own well-funded corner of cognitive science and health science research. Post-traumatic growth, peak experience, creative flow, and the psychology of awe appear routinely in positive psychology and clinical journals with often no reference to their transpersonal-humanistic lineage.

The concerns that transpersonal psychology once held almost alone, such as altered states of consciousness, spiritual emergencies, the need to prioritize psycho-spiritual well-being, and the numinous dimensions of human experience, did not vanish from the discipline of psychology, but rather dispersed into the larger field.

A Death That Wasn’t a Death

The standard academic narrative treats transpersonal psychology’s decline as a failure: too speculative, too based in spiritual or cultural traditions, and too resistant to the empiricism that increasingly defined “credible” psychological science. It’s also true that transpersonal psychology was quite undisciplined in exactly the ways its critics said, but of course that was also its charm and vibrant philosophical depth.

However, fields do not only die by being disproven; they can also die by being absorbed. What is genuinely useful in a marginal field’s questions tends to get extracted, colonized, operationalized, and re-published under headings the mainstream already trusts. So, what I am consistently seeing in academic journals is that the findings are surviving, but the name “transpersonal psychology” is not.

Transpersonal psychology’s fate resembles less a failed theory and more a research program that was quietly stripped for parts by disciplines with better institutional credibility and research methodology. This is not really a loss of ideas, but a loss of authorship for certain key figures such as Grof, Assagioli, and Jung, among others.

Source: Marek Piwnicki / Unsplash

Consider where the field’s core questions live now. Altered states research sits inside psychedelic science and consciousness studies. Additionally, non-pathological spooky experiences, near-death experiences, mystical states, and ego dissolution are increasingly studied inside clinical and health psychology, often under the banner of well-being rather than transcendence.

None of these disciplines typically cite transpersonal psychology as an ancestor. Most researchers publishing in this space today were trained entirely outside it. This is what a genuine diaspora looks like: the population disperses, integrates into new institutions, and largely stops identifying with the place it came from. Wildly enough, the ideas did not fail to convince the field of psychology itself; the ideas convinced the field so thoroughly that they stopped needing their original name.

It is my professional opinion that transpersonal psychology is one of the clearer examples in recent psychological history of a field succeeding by disappearing. The psycho-spiritual questions won, but the name of transpersonal psychology lost. This is worth naming plainly, because the disappearance of a field’s widespread institutional presence is often mistaken for the disappearance of its ideas.

While the ideas themselves are preserved, there is also something lost in this kind of absorption that is deeply unfortunate. Transpersonal psychology brilliantly offered an integrative frame: it treated consciousness, meaning-making, out-of-body experiences, and spiritual frameworks as related expressions of a single deeper concern fluctuating around human wholeness. The downside of its questions being redistributed across a dozen specialized subfields is that the integrative frame disappears along with the name. So, what remains is a set of well-funded and brilliantly published fragments that rarely speak to one another, which is an ongoing issue for the entire modern-day research enterprise.

item.title: Blaming Therapists for Estrangement Misses the Mark
item.description:
Therapy

Blaming Therapists for Estrangement Misses the Mark

A recent article blaming therapists for estrangement draws a skewed conclusion.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • The majority of therapists do not push an estrangement agenda on clients.
  • Ethical therapists work to promote human relationships, not to destroy them.
  • Therapists are guided by a code of ethics, not by online or social media trends.

A Wall Street Journal article with the headline: “Are Therapists to Blame for the Rise of Adults Cutting Off Their Parents?” is circulating widely online and on social media. While the headline is certainly juicy and, no doubt, effective clickbait, there are some inherent problems with the implication that therapists are culpable for a rise in family estrangement.

To be fair, the article attempts to show both sides of the story, despite its less-than-flattering headline, including mentioning that, according to a therapist and professor of family social science, it “should be the tragic exception that you cut off a parent or loved one, not business as usual in therapy.” However, the article also positions therapists as a large part of the issue, claiming that therapists and “estrangement coaches” have been producing a “growing slew of offerings, from quizzes to courses and books, and suggesting that therapists are pushing and perpetuating the narrative of estrangement. But many of these quizzes, assessments, courses, and other estrangement-based content are being presented by social media influencers who may not be actual mental health professionals.

So, the blame, at least in part, is likely misdirected at the therapy profession. An early labeling of estrangement as a "rising trend" was the result of a podcast episode by Oprah Winfrey, not of therapist-created content.

Considering Anecdotal Evidence and Therapist Ethics

The article shares an anecdote of a client who was instructed to cut off her mother, only to regret the decision and feel the therapist had pushed an agenda on her. While we must take seriously the fact that there are unethical therapists who push dubious claims on clients, just as there are unethical doctors who prescribe questionable remedies, we must also understand that this in no way represents the majority of therapists. If a client wishes to discuss estrangement with a family member, it is our ethical duty to listen and help them process the concept, not to instruct, prescribe, or push a specific solution or behavior. This goes for anything that enters the therapy room: our role is never to tell a client what to do (except in serious cases where harm or abuse is evident); rather, it is to act as a supportive force and a help in clarifying and understanding feelings and emotions.

As a clinical social worker, I am bound by my profession’s code of ethics, which lists the “Importance of Human Relationships” as a core value. I interpret this to mean that we believe in and promote the central importance of human relationships, not that we advocate for cutting them off or becoming estranged from loved ones. Of course, there may be exceptions such as in cases of abuse, but, overall, our field guides us to promote repair of relationships, not to suggest destruction of relationships. If a client tells us that they have decided to estrange from a loved one, our role is to help them discuss their decision, to process what this might mean for them, and to act as a support as they figure out how to either maintain or end a relationship—but by no means does this mean that we are instructing or pressuring them to estrange.

We cannot and should not ignore the cases presented in the Journal article of people who have received bad advice from therapists and suffered the cost of estrangement, yet I believe that these therapists represent a small segment of our overall profession, and do not speak for the majority of us, who, as an ethical guideline, do not tell our clients what to do or how to live their lives. While the article sheds light on an important topic, it fails to explore other places outside of the therapy room where the “trend” of estrangement is being pushed and places an unfair culpability on an entire field of helpers.

item.title: Reading Scores Are Falling, Raising Questions About Learning
item.description:
Education

Reading Scores Are Falling, Raising Questions About Learning

A decline in reading shifts the nature of learning.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • There is more reliance on getting information from audiobooks and other short-cuts to reading.
  • Reading and listening each has its advantages in learning.
  • Reading give us the advantage of learning concepts.

Books have played an important part in my life. So I was taken aback when a young cop I know said he doesn’t read. Not that he can’t read; obviously he can since he made it through the police academy. Rather, he prefers information and entertainment via podcasts, audiobooks, PowerPoint and video presentations. I failed to convince him that he was missing a great deal by shunning books.

I thought about him as Gallup and the Bureau of Labor Statistics report that Americans spend less time reading than ever. This is substantiated by teachers who say they must assign shorter texts because students struggle to complete longer assignments; perhaps their students cannot remain focused. Social media doesn’t require attention; it asks only for fleeting attention. Texas has become concerned enough about the decline that it will require schools to institute the reading of entire books from kindergarten through 12th grade. The controversy around the mandate, which goes into effect in a few years, is what’s on the list and what is excluded, not the advisability of the requirement itself.

What is my young acquaintance missing when he declines to read? Each generation, it seems, decries the sorry state of those who follow. Socrates lamented the spread of literacy, saying that writing promoted a false sense of understanding and wisdom as it fostered forgetfulness. It is only face-to-face that people can engage in a dialectical debate, the source of real understanding and wisdom. Furthermore, the written word is static whereas dialogic conversations are dynamic.

In my lifetime, several innovations were condemned as dumbing down children: comic books diverted real books; television watching nudged out reading for pleasure; and computer searches replaced library visits. And now AI can do arcane research instantly and write a more than passable report on whatever you ask of it.

Do technological advances make people dumber? More people became literate because of the printing press; today three-quarters of the world’s population is online, which makes nearly all the world’s facts available in the palm of a hand. More people know more things than ever before. However, information isn’t the same as wisdom.

Reading Versus Listening

What do studies show about learning by reading as opposed to that acquired by listening?

A report in MSU Health Care states that both reading and audiobooks have cognitive benefits. Both modes engage the language-processing brain networks that involve comprehension and meaning-making. However, the two activities differ in this way: Chelsey Bollinger of James Madison University says reading “engages the visual processing systems and areas involved in word recognition and decoding, while listening skips this step and focuses directly on language comprehension.” Reading, it seems, is better for dealing with concepts while listening is fine for taking in information. Print allows a reader to highlight passages or write notes, while audiobooks may make the information more quickly available.

Reading and audiobooks are only tools, and tools are useful only when used properly.

Despite the tsunami of available information, reading comprehension continues to decline. Hofstra professor Alan Singer believes that what correlates with the decline is “the widespread use by children, pre-teens, and teenagers of smartphones, social media, and personalized school laptops.” Coupled with the widespread use of technology, even as early as kindergarten, is digital notetaking. It turns out that hand-written notetaking helps us remember and make sense of information and ideas better than typing notes. A 2026 study by Spanish psychologists said, “The benefit of handwriting with respect to typing is generalized to word identification, word writing, and wording.” They warn educators to be cautious in replacing paper and pencil with digital devices.

New York Public Schools policy and others have banned personal internet-enabled electronic devices. If we are serious about reversing the downward trend in reading, then this is a policy that needs wider acceptance.
